A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Outlier Gradient Analysis research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic-data, noisy-image classification, NLP data-selection, and LLM class-identification experiments, with additional experiments in Appendix B.

after.justification: V3 retains those original empirical results and adds expanded trimming-budget comparisons and distribution-shift experiments in Appendix C.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, the iForest and norm-based methods, and the class-specific LLM forests remain unchanged. Section 8 and Appendix C.8 add an adaptation using OneClassSVM with validation/test samples supplied as inliers, changing the information used to identify detrimental training samples.

E1.justification: V3 adds Folktables ACS-Income and temporal, geographical, and combined distribution-shift scenarios. This extends coverage to tabular income prediction and target-distribution adaptation. The synthetic, CIFAR, ImageNet, GLUE, and LLM benchmark coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Table 11 adds 13 noisy-learning comparators, including Backward-T, Forward-T, VolMinNet, Peer Loss, JoCoR, and ELR, substantially broadening the comparison methods. Gradient Tracing also enters the CIFAR runtime comparison in Table 6, and the expanded budget analysis includes multiple influence baselines absent from v1's budget plot.

E3.justification: The new distribution-shift evaluation explicitly supplies test samples as inliers for OneClassSVM under temporal and geographical shifts. The budget evaluation also expands from a single-method curve to eight methods across three noise regimes and five budgets. The retained main experiments keep their reported model configurations, splits, and training budgets.

E4.justification: V1's limited trimming-threshold analysis in Figure 5 is replaced by a substantially broader sensitivity comparison in v3 Table 5. Appendix C.8 adds tests of adaptation under distribution shift. The tree-count ablation and qualitative image and LLM examples are retained.

E5.justification: V3 Table 4 first supplies five-run standard deviations for Self-LiSSA, Self-DataInf, and the L1/L2 outlier methods, whose means already appeared in v1. Retained run counts are unchanged. Conversely, the replacement budget table reports point values without the shaded bands displayed in v1 Figure 5.

E6.justification: V3 adds extensive budget, noisy-learning baseline, and distribution-shift results. For example, Table 11 reports ELR above all outlier variants on Aggregate and Random noise. Gradient Tracing's ImageNet runtime changes from 6.68e-4 seconds in v1 Table 8 to 23.51 seconds in v3 Table 10. Main Tables 1–3 retain their scores; ImageNet accuracy differences are equivalent rounding.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 removes the higher-order Taylor argument used to claim convexity relaxation. Proposition 3.2 becomes a hypothesis rather than an established equivalence, and Observation 3.1 gains a converged empirical-risk-minimization condition. V3 also corrects the prose interpretation of Equation (2). These revise the foundational mathematical justification.

C1.justification: The title, abstract, contributions, and conclusion narrow the work from an equivalence-based influence-function framework that relaxes convexity to an efficient method for identifying detrimental samples. V3 emphasizes an empirically supported hypothesis and computational savings, withdrawing the central convexity-relaxation contribution.

C2.justification: V3 explicitly interprets LLM identification as a similarity task and discusses the training-distribution limitation motivating validation/test adaptation. It also acknowledges Gradient Tracing's runtime advantage. The budget interpretation changes from identifying 5% as optimal to recommending both 5% and 12.5%, although parts of the new interpretation conflict with Table 5.

D1.justification: Appendix E provides a concrete code-repository address, replacing v1's promise of a future release. A new Section 4 footnote discloses that Gradient Tracing uses only the last checkpoint; this does not establish a changed experiment. Existing hyperparameters, hardware descriptions, and sparse-projection details are largely retained.

R1.justification: V3 substantially revises positioning relative to efficient influence methods, acknowledging Arnoldi/Kronecker-factored approaches and successful non-convex applications. It credits Kim et al. for previously observed detrimental-sample outlyingness and adds ensemble-attribution and noisy-learning literature. The claimed distinction shifts toward the specific detrimental-sample identification task.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution statements, theoretical narrative, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Miscellaneous related work moves to Appendix A, a Discussion section is introduced, and appendix sections are reorganized, including the ImageNet and ResNet-18 analyses.

P2.justification: V3 replaces Figure 5 with a large, grouped budget table and adds Tables 11–12. It expands the uncertainty and runtime tables, transposes the tree-count table, and rearranges several main-text displays. Figures 1–4 retain identical image content despite caption and placement changes.

improvement.justification: V3 improves credibility by withdrawing the unsupported convexity-relaxation argument, broadening baseline comparisons, supplying missing standard deviations, and adding code-access information. The gains remain limited: the new budget discussion incorrectly attributes the best Worst-noise result to L2, although Table 5 reports LiSSA at 84.51 versus L2 at 84.48. The new test-as-inlier distribution-shift evaluation also lacks sufficient local detail about its metric and controls.
